title: Should I renounce to delve myself into important cinema books and docs for the fear of spoilers?

commenti.body: I’m generally of the opinion that if a movie can be spoiled by giving away some plot points then it’s probably not that good anyways. How many of us have favorite films that we watch again and again even though their plot is far from a mystery? Even movies that have shocking twists like The Six Sense still hold up to repeated viewings.

I think I agree with you. The storyline in a movie may differ from its source or if it doesn’t, the screenplay is but only one aspect of a movie that can make it great. It isn’t the only thing. It could be viewed as preparation work for watching a movie. Having the story more or less known to you opens you up to notice more things in a film. 

But I think it also depends on personal taste.
On the other side of the coin, if a film's commentary focuses too much on plot details it's probably not that good either.

Yeah rewatching a movie can be as good or better than the first time but you still only get one opportunity to experience that blind watch. I had the endings to Shutter Island, Oldboy and Fight Club spoiled for me and still really enjoyed those films but every time I showed them to friends and saw their reactions it made me wish I could’ve watched them without knowing the first time. 

Surprise is a very big part of what makes a lot of films great and that can only happen once. You can appreciate the build up to that surprise more the second time but it’s not the same experience.

If you're worried about spoilers, adjust your order of operations. Select a book you want to read, make a list of every movie covered, watch them, then read the book. Then you also have more context and understanding for whatever the author is discussing.

I think it's great when you can go into a movie unspoiled, and certainly try to avoid springing spoilers on people out of the blue when talking about movies (or shows, or books). 

That said, spoilers are fixated on narrative surprises in part because that's a really easy thing to talk about — but a movie. Even most narrative cinema does not exist primarily to deliver a story. A story, with whatever surprises it holds, is one element of a movie, but it's often not the most important part. 

There's nothing wrong with reading film history, theory, or criticism and not caring if you find out things that might have surprised you. Part of being familiar with any art form is finding out what kinds of things become "common knowledge." 

Most people now see *Psycho* knowing things that were surprises to most people seeing it for the first time. That hasn't lessened its influence, or ruined the movie. Is it nice to go in completely blind? Sure! If I was talking to someone who knew nothing about it, I'd avoid revealing much and encourage them to check it out without learning much more. But it obviously isn't necessary. 

All of this to say: If spoilers don't bother you, there's no reason to try to make them bother you. Read the books. If there's discussion of a movie you think you might want to go into unspoiled, stop reading and watch the movie first — but you're not "doing it wrong" if you learn things that might have been a nice surprise.

I think diving into these books will probably help you change your relationship and perspective on cinema. It will help you stop seeing cinema as 'filmed scenarios,' which will likely make you place much less importance on Things like that.

I think you're going to find out that even if an analysis of a particular film reveals the plot etc, you'll probably not be thinking about that while watching the film.  At least that's my experience.  

The whole "spoiler" thing kicked off in the mainstream probably around The 6th Sense but that was because of a huge reveal that completely changed your experience of the movie.  Since then we've gotten so connected via social media etc and so hyper-sensitive that people consider anything to be a spoiler.  My point is that a lot of those things don't actually spoil the movie.

I studied film and worked in the industry so I came up around film nerds (I include myself) that were a lot more sensitive than most people, so it's a little funny to see how this has become mainstream over the years.

I watch movies as I read about them in those books, for example I watched all of Tarkovsky's movies as I read his book.  It is impossible to avoid all spoilers, but the narrative is often secondary.  The more I learn, the more things I want to see and I don't care if I already know what will happen in those movies.

I’ve seen a great majority of “the classics” and as a result I don’t get much out of documentaries like Mark Cousins’ *The Story of Film*. Their whole purpose is to introduce people with a more casual interest or with less experience watching film than me. I would say watch those now before you know too much.
